blocks.text: Imagine trying to optimize a complex program without a clear map of its execution paths. Control flow graphs (CFGs) provide that map, making it easier to analyze and optimize code.

blocks.markdown: Control Flow Graphs (CFGs) are a fundamental concept in compiler design, representing the flow of control within a program. They are used to partition code into basic blocks and illustrate the paths that execution can take through a program.

blocks.title: Basic Block
blocks.text: A basic block is a sequence of consecutive statements in which flow of control enters at the beginning and leaves at the end without halt or possibility of branching except at the end.

blocks.markdown: To construct a CFG, we first partition a sequence of code into basic blocks. This involves identifying leaders, which are the first instructions of basic blocks. A leader can be the first instruction of the program, the target of a jump, or the instruction following a conditional or unconditional jump.

blocks.title: Identifying Basic Blocks
blocks.prompt: Consider the following sequence of three-address code. Identify the basic blocks.

steps.text: 1. Identify the leaders in the code sequence: the first instruction, any instruction that is the target of a jump, and any instruction following a jump.
2. Partition the code into basic blocks based on these leaders.

blocks.answer: The basic blocks are: [B1: i1, i2], [B2: i3, i4], [B3: i5].

blocks.markdown: Once basic blocks are identified, a CFG can be constructed. In a CFG, nodes represent basic blocks, and directed edges represent possible flow of control between blocks.

blocks.title: Control Flow Graph (CFG)
blocks.text: A CFG is a directed graph where nodes are basic blocks and edges represent control flow paths between these blocks.

blocks.title: Constructing a CFG
blocks.prompt: Construct a CFG from the following three-address code: B1: i1; i2; goto B2; B2: i3; if x goto B3; B3: i4.

steps.text: 1. Identify the basic blocks: B1, B2, B3.
2. Draw nodes for each basic block.
3. Add directed edges based on the control flow: B1 to B2, B2 to B3, B2 to itself (if x is true).

blocks.answer: The CFG consists of nodes B1, B2, B3 with edges: B1 -> B2, B2 -> B3, and a self-loop on B2.

blocks.caption: Components of a Control Flow Graph

blocks.markdown: Loops in a CFG are identified by finding strongly connected components or back edges. A loop is a path that starts and ends at the same node, with all nodes in the path having a path to the start node.

blocks.title: Identifying Loops
blocks.text: In a CFG, a loop is present if there is a path from a node back to itself, forming a cycle.

points: CFGs partition code into basic blocks and represent control flow.
Nodes in a CFG are basic blocks; edges represent control paths.
Loops in CFGs are identified by cycles or back edges.
